reason: The provided sources support over 15 distinct claims with multiple site citations, including surprising details about naming, fuel-saving maneuvers, and its record-breaking longevity.
story: NASA’s 2001 Mars Odyssey is the ultimate space survivor. Originally called "ARES," the mission was renamed after NASA contacted legendary author Arthur C. Clarke, who personally blessed the tribute to his masterpiece. To save fuel, Odyssey didn’t use its main engines to reach orbit; it "surfed" the Martian atmosphere, using air resistance to slow down in a maneuver called aerobraking. For over 23 years, it has served as the "interplanetary internet," relaying roughly 85% of data from rovers like Spirit and Opportunity. It even provided a critical lifeline during Curiosity’s "seven minutes of terror" landing. Despite its radiation sensor being fried by a solar storm in 2003, it remains the longest-continually active spacecraft at another planet. Today, it still circles Mars every few hours, mapping hidden ice and minerals to help future astronauts prepare for the first human steps on the Red Planet.
angle: NASA's oldest active Mars orbiter is an 'interplanetary internet' that has survived for over 23 years and saved a record-breaking landing.

claims.claim: Mars Odyssey launched from Cape Canaveral on April 7, 2001
The spacecraft reached Mars in October 2001
Odyssey is the longest-continually active spacecraft in orbit around a planet other than Earth
The mission was named as a tribute to Arthur C. Clarke and his work 2001: A Space Odyssey
Arthur C. Clarke personally approved the use of the name for the NASA mission
The spacecraft used a technique called aerobraking, using atmospheric drag to circularize its orbit
Aerobraking allowed the mission to save significant fuel and launch on a smaller, less expensive rocket
Odyssey discovered vast reservoirs of water ice buried just beneath the Martian surface
The orbiter used a Gamma Ray Spectrometer to detect hydrogen, a signature for water ice
The THEMIS instrument provides thermal and visible imaging to map Martian minerals
Odyssey acts as a communications relay, or 'interplanetary internet,' for missions on the surface
The spacecraft relayed approximately 85% of the data from the Spirit and Opportunity rovers
The MARIE radiation instrument failed in 2003 after being hit by a solar particle event
The mission had an expected development and launch cost of approximately $297 million
Odyssey broke the record for the longest-serving spacecraft at Mars in December 2010
The orbiter’s propellant reserves are estimated to last until at least late 2025 or 2026
Odyssey provided critical data relay during the Curiosity rover's high-stakes landing in 2012
The orbiter helped identify and select landing sites for the Curiosity and Phoenix missions
Odyssey was maneuvered into a new orbit in 2014 to observe surface temperature changes after sunrise and sunset
The mission is managed by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and was built by Lockheed Martin

disputed: The arrival date is cited as either October 23 or October 24, 2001, depending on the time zone (PDT vs UTC).

The exact percentage of data relayed from the Spirit and Opportunity rovers varies by report, with some citing 85% and others over 95%; a script should use the more conservative 85% or attribute the higher figure to specific mission updates.
